title: The Sun Krishna Has Set
story:
When Vidura put his question, the silence that answered it lasted a long moment. He had asked Uddhava to speak of Krishna — of his life, his deeds, his end — and Uddhava, who had served Krishna since he was five years old and had grown old in that service, seemed for a while to have forgotten that anyone was waiting. He sat on the bank of the Yamuna with his eyes closed, sunk in the sweetness of Krishna's feet, his limbs trembling with devotion, tears slipping from beneath his lids. Then, slowly, he wiped his eyes, and when he looked up he was smiling.

"The sun has set," he said. "Krishna has set. What good news can I bring to houses stripped of their fortune? Wretched is this world, and more wretched still the Yadavas — who lived with Hari, ate with him, fought beside him, and never knew him."

This was the grief that had been gathering in Uddhava since the news of Prabhasa reached him. The Yadavas had been no ordinary clan. They were subtle men, masters at reading a glance, mature in counsel, devoted to Krishna alone. And yet the Lord's own maya had touched them; the very magic by which he had played among mortals had closed their eyes. They had lived inside the miracle and never once recognised it.

Now that the miracle was over, memory came back to Uddhava in fragments he could not stop. He remembered the Rajasuya of Yudhishthira, when the three worlds had looked upon Krishna and found their eyes blessed by the sight. He remembered the love that spilled from Krishna's laughing glance in the play of the rasa, the look that had given worth to everyone it fell on. Who among the gods, he asked, could ever forget the dust of his lotus feet? At that same Rajasuya, even Shishupala — who had hated Krishna all his life — had reached perfection, drawn by that hatred into a fixed gazing at his enemy. And in the great battles, the heroes of the earth had fallen looking upon the lotus of Krishna's face.

That was the strangest part of his sorrow. Enemies had won release by fixing their minds on Krishna, however unwillingly. The whole world had been given the sight of him. Only his own kinsmen — the ones who had been closest — had been struck blind.

He spoke too of the Lord's birth in Vasudeva's house, the play of the Unborn taking on birth, and of how Krishna, before setting out on some errand, had bowed at his parents' feet. The memory choked him. "Who could ever forget the dust of his lotus feet?" he said again. "And we — we lived our whole lives beside him."

Vidura listened and asked nothing more. This was why he had come down to the bank of the Yamuna: to learn from Uddhava the deeds of Krishna, the story of the one whose coming had changed the world and whose going had darkened it. And Uddhava, wiping his eyes once more, drew a breath and began to tell it — the long tale that Vidura would carry away with him, and that would be told again and again long after both of them were gone.

He stopped once, and said something strange: that the man seated before him on the riverbank was no ordinary minister, but one without equal, a lord of the three worlds, every desire fulfilled by the fortune of his own sovereignty. Vidura did not answer. In the world after Krishna, Uddhava seemed to be saying, even the greatest souls stood disguised, and only love could recognise them.

The river moved past them, unhurried, the same water that had once carried the little boat of the cowherd boy's infancy. Uddhava's voice steadied as he spoke, as if the telling itself were a kind of returning. The sun had set, but the remembering had begun.
reflection: Uddhava's sorrow is the sorrow of proximity without recognition: the Yadavas had what the whole world longed for and could not see it. The Bhagavata frames its telling through his grief, as if the story of Krishna can only be told properly by someone who has first understood what it cost to be near him and to know him only after he was gone.
